verdicts.note: Raw PDF text extracted with pypdf from the live espivblogs copy (HTTP 200, 1,538,986 bytes, 253 pages). In the Tolkien sample of 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose': 'Sentences: 4 plus a paragraph break / Bars: 15 / Words: 72 / Words of one syllable: 45'. The hundred-syllable limb is supported: 'The passages are of one hundred syllables to the dagger (anything past the dagger is not counted)', and the summary tables are headed 'Per 100-syllable sample:', where 'Number of one-syllable words' lists 'Tolkien: 45' and 'Number of words' lists 'Austen, Tolkien: 72'. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: The samples are far too small and the method of counting stresses too subjective for any conclusions at all to be drawn
verdicts.note: Verbatim on the page immediately after the comparison tables and the 'Various interesting factoids emerge' list. The claim's 'her stress-counting' renders the page's 'the method of counting stresses'; both limbs (samples too small; counting too subjective) are on the page in one sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: That Jane Austen's stress-count is almost the same as that of the textbook is, however, a good indication that merely counting stresses is not going to give us any solid indications of the quality--in all senses--of the prose
verdicts.note: Verbatim, immediately following the 'far too small' sentence. Both limbs supported: the Austen/textbook near-match (tables give Austen 33, Craig 32) and the inference about quality. Nuance, not a defect: the page hedges as 'a good indication that merely counting stresses is not going to give us any SOLID indications' where the claim says 'shows ... cannot indicate' -- the hedge is carried inside the quoted words themselves.

verdicts.trueWording: that in even a readable textbook more than half the words are polysyllables
verdicts.note: Verbatim, third bullet of the 'Various interesting factoids emerge' list. Corroborated by her own counts for the Craig et al. textbook sample: 'Words: 52.5 / Words of one syllable: 25', i.e. more than half polysyllabic.

verdicts.trueWording: that Mark Twain uses more one-syllable words than a folktale
verdicts.note: Verbatim, second bullet of the 'Various interesting factoids emerge' list. Corroborated by the table 'Number of one-syllable words, most to fewest: Twain: 72 / "Three Bears": 62'.

verdicts.trueWording: that Woolf writes the shortest sentences of the lot and Austen the longest
verdicts.note: Verbatim, fourth bullet of the 'Various interesting factoids emerge' list. The claim's 'of the eight samples' is supported: the tables enumerate exactly eight samples ('Three Bears', Woolf, Tolkien, Twain, Stein, Darwin, Austen, Craig). Source-internal tension worth flagging but not a claim defect, since the claim reports what Le Guin's counts are said to show and the page asserts it as a factoid emerging from those counts: her per-passage counts give Darwin 1 sentence in 77 words against Austen 1 sentence in 72, so within the 100-syllable window Darwin's single sentence is the longer; both samples are cut mid-sentence at the dagger.

verdicts.trueWording: But the power of deliberate repetition in a narrative is both great and legitimate
verdicts.note: Verbatim, closing sentence of the 'Repetition of Words or Phrases' section, exactly the section the claim names.

Verbatim, opening the 'BEYOND STRESS / Long Prose Rhythms' section the claim names ('Rhythm is repetition. In a prose narrative, which must "move" with the events it tells...'). The sentence occurs twice in the book -- again in the following essay, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' -- so the attribution is safe either way.

verdicts.trueWording: Its coherence is established by inner references and backward-looking or forward-looking semirepetitions
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the 'Repetition of Images, Actions, Moods, and Themes' section, the section the claim names. The claim's 'backward- or forward-looking semirepetitions' compresses the page's 'backward-looking or forward-looking semirepetitions'; the referent of 'Its' is 'a well-written narrative', so the claim's 'a narrative's coherence' is exact.

verdicts.trueWording: If the rhythms become predictable, the coherence of the story is mechanical
verdicts.note: Verbatim, two sentences after the semirepetitions sentence, in the same 'Repetition of Images, Actions, Moods, and Themes' section. The claim's 'warns' matches the passage's contrastive structure (pure repetition loses drive; predictable rhythms make coherence mechanical; varied repetitions give forward movement).

verdicts.trueWording: textbook prose tends to hobble along clogged by a superfluity of egregiously unnecessary and understressed polysyllables
verdicts.note: Verbatim in 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings', in the stress-ratio passage on the essay's early pages, exactly where the claim's page hint places it. The essay's own headnote supports the 2001 attribution: it 'happily found a home in Karen Haber's anthology of writing on Tolkien, Meditations on Middle Earth, published in 2001'. The claim drops 'egregiously' from its paraphrase but the quote field carries it.

verdicts.trueWording: In poetry ... one syllable out of every two or three has a beat on it ... In narrative prose, that ratio goes down to one beat in two to four
verdicts.note: Both limbs verbatim and adjacent: 'In poetry, by and large, one syllable out of every two or three has a beat on it: Tum ta Tum ta ta Tum Tum ta, and so on... . In narrative prose, that ratio goes down to one beat in two to four: ta Tum tatty Tum ta Tum tatatty, and so on... .'

verdicts.trueWording: Tolkien's prose runs to the normal narrative ratio of one stress every two to four syllables
verdicts.note: Verbatim, the sentence immediately after the textbook-prose sentence of claim 175. The page continues: 'In passages of intense action and feeling the ratio may get pretty close to 50 percent, like poetry, but still, except for Tom, it is irregular, it can't be scanned' -- a qualification the claim does not contradict, since it reports the normal ratio.

verdicts.trueWording: The speech of the elves and noble folk such as Aragorn has a dignified, often stately gait, but not a regular stress-beat
verdicts.note: Verbatim, in the passage on metric passages in the Trilogy the claim's page hint names ('If there are other metric passages in the Trilogy, I've missed them.'). Every limb -- elves and noble folk, Aragorn as the example, dignified/often stately gait, absence of a regular stress-beat -- is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: The narrative moves in balanced cadences in passages of epic action ... but it remains pure prose
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the same paragraph as claim 178: 'The narrative moves in balanced cadences in passages of epic action, with a majestic sweep reminiscent of epic poetry, but it remains pure prose.' Both limbs (balanced cadences in epic action; remains pure prose) supported.
